title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Runbooks (Comprehensive)
author: Evelyn Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates serving runtime guidance for Redwood Inference: architecture, kernel & scheduling design, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes guidance, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki links. It is the canonical reference used by runtime engineers, SRE, and performance-focused product partners.

Goals
- Describe the runtime architecture and key subsystems.
- Provide kernel scheduling rationale and tunable knobs.
- Share profiling and benchmarking playbooks with examples.
- Provide standardized release note checklist and known-issues catalog entries.
- Include runbooks for common incidents and operational tasks.

Audience
- Serving runtime engineers
- Platform SREs
- Performance QA and applied ML engineers
- Release managers for runtime builds

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: Serving Runtime team (eng-serving-runtime)
- On-call escalation: Eng SRE rotation (see /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks)
- Pager: channel #runtime-pager and PagerDuty service ID: PD-RT-01

1) Runtime architecture (high level)

Summary
The runtime is a modular, GPU-first inference engine that supports transformer-based models (FP16, INT8 quantized variants), multi-tenant routing, progressive KV cache, and continuous batching. The core modules are: loader, graph executor, kernel selector, scheduler, cache manager, telemetry agent, and admission controller.

Diagram (text)
Client -> Admission Controller -> Scheduler -> Worker Pool (Loader -> Kernel Selector -> Executor -> KV Cache) -> Embedding/Storage -> Telemetry + Tracing

Key design decisions
- Separate kernel selection from scheduling to allow cross-worker kernel specialization and shared kernel cache.
- Continuous batching at admission controller using size/time windows with backpressure. Default window: 8ms or 64 tokens.
- KV cache is sharded per model shard and supports prefix-aware eviction; persistent in-memory state on worker for warm-start.
- Two-level routing: tenant-aware policy (cost/latency tier) and capability-aware policy (model variant compatibility).

SLOs and performance targets
| Metric | Target (p95) | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| Token latency (interactive) | 80ms | 8k context, RAL=high-priority path |
| Token latency (background) | 200ms | batch-friendly routes |
| Throughput (max per-GPU) | 8000 tokens/s | depends on model and quantization |
| Availability | 99.95% | per-dedicated-pool SLA |

Service names and components
- runtime-admission (k8s deployment: runtime-admission vX.Y)
- runtime-scheduler (statefulset: runtime-scheduler)
- runtime-worker (DaemonSet on GPU nodes)
- runtime-telemetry (sidecar + exporter)

2) Kernel selection & scheduling

Goal
Choose the fastest correct kernel variant given: model operator (attention, matmul), sequence length distribution, quantization mode, and hardware topology. Schedule work to minimize tail latency while maximizing GPU utilization.

Kernel selection rules (priority order)
1. Exact-architecture specialized kernels (best)
2. Fallback optimized kernels (reduced precision friendly)
3. Generic kernels (last resort)

Examples
- For causal attention, prefer fused attention kernels for A100/MI250 with seq_len <= 4096.
- For quantized INT8 variants, prefer kernels with 8-bit GEMM + compensation path. If compensation increases latency > 15%, route to FP16 path for latency-sensitive tiers.

Scheduling knobs (config YAML example)
```yaml
scheduler:
  admission_window_ms: 8
  max_batch_size: 64
  preempt_low_priority_after_ms: 120
  kv_cache_eviction_policy: lru_per_shard
  worker_affinity: "gpu_type:ampere||gpu_family:mi"
```

Placement and topology awareness
- Scheduler respects socket and NVLink locality: pack worker threads preferring same GPU NUMA group to avoid PCIe hops.
- Use GPU capacity binning: small (<=24GB), medium (24-48GB), large (>=48GB). Kernel selection considers available memory headroom.

Backpressure & admission control
- Admission controller throttles by token-QPS and active-batches. When active_batches > 1024, admission switches to sampling mode and returns 429 or a queued handle depending on tenant policy.

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

Goal: Diagnose latency spikes and identify kernel hotspots or memory pressure issues.

Pre-setup checklist
- Reproduce workload on staging with synthetic trace (see examples below).
- Ensure perf tooling installed: nsight-systems, nvprof (deprecated), nvtx annotations, PyTorch profiler (if using PT exporter), and runtime-specific telemetry enabled.
- Collect a minimum of 60s of steady-state traffic for batch-sensitive issues.

Step-by-step profiling playbook
1. Validate baseline: capture p50/p95 token latency and throughput in metrics (Prometheus).
2. Start coarse profiler: nsight-systems snapshot for 30s. Capture GPU kernel timeline and PCIe events.
3. If kernel-level contention suspected, enable nvtx markers in runtime and record per-call durations.
4. Correlate NVTX regions with Prometheus traces and spans (trace IDs).
5. If memory OOM or suboptimal allocation observed, run cuda-memcheck / check unified memory thrashing.
6. If scheduler-level queuing observed, capture admission queue depth and batch size histogram.

Common indicators and remediations
- Long GPU memcpy stalls between kernels: check pipelining; enable kernel fusion or increase batch window slightly.
- Small kernels dominating time (kernel launch overhead): increase batching or switch to fused kernels.
- KV cache eviction churn: increase cache capacity or adjust lru_per_shard thresholds.

Example CLI commands
- nsight-systems: sudo nsys profile --sample=cpu --trace=cuda --output=profile.nsys ./runtime-worker --config ./conf.yaml
- Inspect metrics: curl -s http://prometheus:9090/api/v1/query?query='histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(runtime_token_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le))' | jq .

4) Benchmarking suite (standard tests)

Scope
Benchmarks target token throughput, latency distribution, memory utilization, end-to-end service-level SLO compliance, and cost-per-token estimates. Use both synthetic and representative production traces.

Canonical workloads
- Small-chat: 512 tokens, batch-friendly, 20 RPS per instance.
- Long-context: 32k token window, low RPS, heavy KV cache.
- Embedding-bulk: short tokens (<=128), high concurrency.
- RAG/LLM-chained pipelines: includes retrieval and embedding steps; measures end-to-end latency.

Benchmark harness (example commands)
```bash
# run synthetic benchmark against local worker
bench-runner --target http://localhost:8080/generate --config bench/small-chat.yaml --duration 300s --output results/small-chat.json
```

Example results table (artifact stored under s3://bench-results/yyyy-mm-dd)
| workload | p50 latency | p95 latency | tokens/sec | notes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| small-chat | 35ms | 82ms | 6100 | default FP16 path |
| long-context | 120ms | 420ms | 1500 | KV warm-up required |

Cost estimation guidance
- Collect GPU utilization and per-GPU-hour cost. tokens/sec normalized by cost gives cost-per-1M-tokens. Use bench harness to compute.

5) Release notes & versioning guidance

When cutting a runtime release follow this checklist:
1. Include semantic version and build id (e.g., runtime v2.14.0+build.20280304).
2. Document kernel changes and new kernel-selection heuristics.
3. Include benchmark deltas (p50/p95) for canonical workloads and note any SLO regressions.
4. Security and compatibility notes (CUDA/toolkit versions, driver requirements).
5. Rollout guidance (canary percentage, metrics to monitor, rollback criteria).

Rollout example
- Canary: 2 nodes (10% traffic) for 2 hours. If p95 increases by >15% or error rate >0.5%, abort.
- Gradual: 10% -> 30% -> 60% over 6h with health checks every 15m.

Release notes template (snippet)
```
Title: runtime v2.14.0
Highlights:
- Added fused attention kernel for MI250 (seq <= 4096) -> 18% p95 improvement on small-chat.
- Improved kv_cache LRU per-shard to reduce eviction churn for long-context workloads.
Benchmarks:
- small-chat: p95 -18% (82ms -> 67ms)
- long-context: p95 +5% (420ms -> 441ms) — flagged for follow-up.
Compatibility:
- Requires CUDA 12.2 and driver >= 535.xx
```

6) Known issues (active catalog)

Use the following entries to seed the known-issues board. Update status field in issue tracker.

- ISSUE-RT-102: MI250 fused attention regressions on seq_len=8192. Status: investigating. Workaround: route seq_len>4096 to fp16 path. Owner: Marco Alvarez.
- ISSUE-RT-118: KV cache noisy eviction under bursty rerank workloads. Status: mitigated (kv_cache tuning). Owner: Rajiv Menon.
- ISSUE-RT-130: Occasional 429s during global autoscaler events. Status: resolved in admission v1.8. Owner: Evelyn Chen.

How to file a known issue
1. Create an internal ticket in JIRA with label runtime-known-issue.
2. Add reproducible trace, profile, metric snapshots, and affected builds.
3. Link this page in the JIRA and update related_pages list.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

Runbook: High token-latency (p95 spike)
1. Triage: check alert #runtime-high-p95 -> runbook invoked.
2. Confirm scope: single node / pool / global (Prometheus label: pool_id).
3. Collect recent profile: nsys snapshot from affected worker.
4. Check admission queue depth, batch size distribution and KV cache hit rate.
5. If kernel stalls present -> scale up worker pool and roll to known-good build.
6. If admission backlog due to upstream burst -> enable burst mode in admission and increase backlog window.
7. Post-incident: file postmortem if >30m impact; include timeline and remediation.

Runbook: GPU OOM on worker startup
1. Check node allocatable memory and driver compatibility (nvidia-smi).
2. Inspect pod events: kubectl describe pod <worker-pod>.
3. If model shard allocation fails, fallback to smaller shard or restart with --model-cache-size reduced.
4. For persistent OOM after restart, cordon node and drain; mark node hardware-health for inspection.

Runbook: Kernel regression post-release
1. Reproduce on staging using the benchmark harness and the offending CI artifact.
2. Bisect to commit introducing kernel change (git bisect across runtime-kernels).
3. If kernel regression confirmed, revert kernel change and patch.
